claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC HEA nanoscale multilayers under sustained loading is governed by dislocation accumulation at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Individual layer thickness modulates the available dislocation slip length.
Individual layer thickness modulates stress concentration at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Severe lattice distortion influences dislocation transmission and absorption at interfaces.
Local short-range chemical order influences dislocation transmission and absorption at interfaces.
The proposed starting multilayers have well-defined, coherent, as-deposited FCC/BCC interfaces.
Atom-probe tomography and local strain mapping can characterize interfacial lattice distortion and short-range ordering relevant to the hypothesis.
FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Layer thickness controls the degree of interfacial dislocation pile-up and subsequent slip transmission.
Sustained loading causes dislocations to nucleate and accumulate at nanoscale FCC/BCC interfaces.
Thinner layers provide a shorter dislocation slip length.
The shorter slip length in thinner layers reduces stress concentration at interfaces.
Reduced interfacial stress concentration in thinner layers promotes more frequent dislocation transmission.
More frequent dislocation transmission produces a spatially distributed plastic response.
Thicker layers promote pronounced dislocation pile-ups.
Pronounced dislocation pile-ups are associated with localized deformation hotspots.
Thinner multilayers will exhibit more homogeneous plastic-strain distributions than thicker multilayers.
Thicker multilayers will exhibit more localized plastic-deformation hotspots than thinner multilayers.
Variations in local lattice distortion should correspond to changes in creep behavior.
An intermediate-thickness FCC/BCC HEA multilayer baseline exhibits moderate creep rates and conventional dislocation distributions.
